prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The map supports a coarse near-to-far layout: the floor extends forward into the mall corridor, while walls and storefronts form more distant vertical boundaries; brighter regions indicate that people entering from the right become very close to the camera. In frames 1–2, the people on the far left are roughly 4–7 m away and the nearby wall/display is about 2–4 m away, while much of the open floor lies between them and the wearer. In frame 3, a person is partly out of view on the right at about 0.5–1.5 m; in frame 4, another person is approximately 1–2 m ahead-right with a second person several metres farther down the corridor; by frame 5, the nearest person and carried object fill the right side at well under 1 m, within the wearer’s arm’s reach. The depth rendering makes the rapid approach and near-camera occlusion clearer than RGB alone, but its broad gradients, clipped bright silhouettes, dark storefront areas, and inconsistent boundaries make exact distances and separations unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance map identifies several people in frame 1 on the left at roughly 4–7 m, separated from one another by about 0.5–2 m, plus a wall-mounted TV/display left of centre; it also isolates a farther person near the corridor opening. Across frames 3–5, it shows a person entering from the upper-right edge, then a large person mask ahead-right, and finally a person so close on the right that the body is heavily cropped and within about 1 m of the wearer. Mask position and scale make left/right ordering, partial out-of-view bodies, overlap, and the transition from distant to near easier to see than in RGB, but the map gives no direct metric depth or reliable facing direction. It is unreliable where labels fragment into tiny duplicate person instances around frame 4, where masks merge or omit body parts, and where nearby objects—including the spotted item in frame 5—are unlabelled; therefore distances must be inferred from RGB and apparent mask size.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is entirely black in all five frames, so it provides no detected body or hand joints, no facing direction, and no evidence about whether anyone looks toward the camera wearer. It also cannot establish limb positions, interpersonal reach, or whether the person and object closest on the right in frames 3–5 are within anyone else’s arm’s reach. Relative scene layout, occlusion, and approach must therefore come only from the RGB, depth, and segmentation strips: distant people remain on the left in frame 1, while a person enters from the right, grows larger, and becomes strongly cropped at close range by frame 5. The absent skeletons are unreliable as a representation of the visible people, especially the large nearby figures, whose partial framing and occlusion may have prevented pose detection.
